strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying persuasive communication as a critical gap in existing SDG agents
Conceptually interesting Stackelberg competition formulation providing intuitive grounding for turn-based dialogue
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse SDGs with 4-5 baselines per game
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of complete reward function and training-based vs prompt-based refinement
Demonstrated generalization across different backend LLMs (GPT-5, Qwen3-14B) without retraining
Pragmatic two-stage architecture leveraging both API-based and open-source LLMs
Clear presentation with informative figures and qualitative case studies
weaknesses: Loose application of Stackelberg theory: claims local leader-follower optimization leads to global game success but provides only intuition, not rigorous proof (Eq. 13)
Critical train-test information mismatch: rewards computed with full information (rt+1) during training but unavailable at inference, creating significant distribution shift
Validity of Measurer as reward signal questionable: frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct assumed to accurately model followers using different LLMs, but variable generalization (Figure 4) suggests otherwise
Unfair baseline comparisons: Refiner applied on top of existing baselines adds optimization layer baseline authors didn't access; no equivalent computational budget comparison
Self-play dataset potential bias: training data from only 3 LLMs may optimize for their specific instruction-following patterns rather than general persuasion principles
Limited analysis of learned behaviors: no linguistic pattern analysis, no failure cases, unsupported claims about learning 'model-agnostic principles'
Incomplete reproducibility: prompt sensitivity not analyzed, hyperparameter selection (LoRA rank 16, n=8, β=0.04) not justified, no code/data release, dependency on proprietary models
Reward function concerns: no analysis of edge cases (very high/low probabilities), potential issues with different target response lengths, token probability normalization
Evaluation gaps: no confidence intervals or significance tests for reported performance differences; unclear agent sampling procedure in evaluation games

strengths: Novel framing of persuasive communication in SDGs as Stackelberg competition
Consistent empirical improvements across three diverse social deduction games
Comprehensive experiments including ablations on reward function, cross-LLM generalization, and two-stage refinement
Thorough presentation with extensive implementation details, appendices, and qualitative case studies
Complementary nature demonstrated across multiple baselines without requiring retraining
weaknesses: Critical training-inference mismatch: rewards computed using oracle next-player role information unavailable at test time, with impact not analyzed

Questionable fit of Stackelberg framework to SDGs: assumes sequential commitment absent in fluid discussion phases; lacks rigorous justification that local follower optimization improves global game outcomes
Circular reward design: optimizing to make LLM-identified 'desired' responses more likely may simply learn to echo backend preferences rather than discover persuasion principles
Poor proxy for follower: using frozen Llama-3-8B Measurer to approximate actual Gemini/GPT follower responses ignores model-specific differences; Table 3 results suggest inaccuracy

Unclear attribution of improvements: cannot distinguish whether wins come from Stackelberg optimization, better backend LLM (Gemini), or general utterance refinement, with confounded experimental design
Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error analysis across all results; win rates estimated without uncertainty quantification
Small self-play dataset (4,000 instances from 500 games) with no coverage analysis; data from vanilla agents may not reflect diverse gameplay distribution
Limited analysis of what is learned: beyond case studies, minimal insight into linguistic features or patterns distinguishing effective refinements; no error analysis or failure modes
Weak theoretical justification: Equation 13 and 'first-order approximation' claims (Appendix B.1.3) are hand-wavy rather than rigorous mathematical argument
Reproducibility concerns: heavy dependence on closed-source API LLMs (Gemini, GPT-4o, Claude) and no code release mentioned

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: clearly articulates the gap in prior work on persuasive communication in SDG agents
Elegant theoretical framework: Stackelberg competition provides intuitive and systematic formalization of turn-based dialogue
Sound methodology: pragmatic two-stage approach (API backend + open-source Refiner) with appropriate use of GRPO
Strong and consistent empirical results: 5-10% win-rate improvements across three diverse SDGs with multiple baselines
Excellent generalization: method works effectively on unseen backend LLMs (GPT-5, Qwen3-14B) without retraining, suggesting model-agnostic learning
Comprehensive experiments: well-designed ablations on reward function variants and detailed analysis of two-stage refinement necessity
Clear presentation: well-structured paper with effective figures and logical flow
weaknesses: Critical model mismatch: uses frozen open-source LLM (Llama-3-8B) to estimate API-LLM follower responses without theoretical justification—empirical success doesn't validate this conceptual gap
Weak theoretical justification for Stackelberg as first-order approximation: no quantitative bounds or empirical validation of approximation quality, only qualitative intuition
Intent identification (Eq. 1) completely unanalyzed: no evaluation of identification quality, no ablation on whether better intents improve performance—this critical pipeline component is neglected
Training-evaluation distributional mismatch: training uses vanilla agent utterances while evaluation uses refined utterances; no discussion of covariate shift or validation of robustness
Lack of statistical rigor: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or statistical tests reported; main Table 1 results lack frequency controls that Table 2 provides
Limited analysis of learned patterns: no systematic study of linguistic features in refined utterances, case studies are anecdotal, no characterization of persuasion strategies
Insufficient exploration of negative-only variant: explanation for why negative-only fails is hand-wavy; suggests reward function may be fragile but this isn't investigated
Limited methodological novelty: applies existing GRPO algorithm without innovation in RL methodology; core contribution is problem formulation and Stackelberg framing
Scope and generalization concerns: approach specific to turn-based dialogue games with one Refiner per game; unclear cross-game or cross-domain applicability
Reproducibility gaps: game state approximation at phase boundaries unclear, hyperparameter choices (n=8, β=0.04, 1e-6 learning rate) lack justification, no code availability mentioned

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine gap in SDG literature by focusing on persuasive communication rather than just strategy selection
Clear and intuitive methodology: Three-step framework (Intent Identification, Impact Measurement, Strategy Optimization) is well-designed and easy to follow
Pragmatic technical approach: Uses GRPO to avoid preference data/critic models; two-stage architecture leveraging API and open-source LLMs is effective

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Four benchmarks, multiple strong baselines, ablations on reward variants and hyperparameters, cross-LLM generalization studies, human evaluation with proper protocols, qualitative case studies, and persuasion effectiveness analysis
Consistent improvements across domains: Gains demonstrated across Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW, and Sotopia, suggesting reasonable generalizability
Good reproducibility support: Clear implementation details, hyperparameters, training procedures, and prompts in appendices; code/data release promised
weaknesses: Weak theoretical foundation: Claim that local Stackelberg optimization creates beneficial cascade lacks rigorous justification; counterexamples exist (utterances convincing next player but alienating later players); relationship to global game outcomes is informal first-order approximation

Train-test mismatch on hidden information: Method uses next player's hidden role r_{t+1} during reward computation at training time but not at inference; justification is circular; no analysis of performance degradation from this mismatch

Modest and inconsistent improvements: Gains range from 2.6-6.1% across games; some configurations show degradation (Avalon Good: 70.5%→73.1% is improvement but context shows variance); no statistical significance testing despite 500 matches per game
Computational cost and scalability: Requires 50 GPU-hours per game; necessitates training separate model per scenario; limits practical applicability to new domains

Reward signal design concerns: K=3 is empirically validated but somewhat arbitrary; using Qwen2.5-72B to approximate Gemini-2.5-Flash responses is unvalidated approximation; intent identification via prompting is non-deterministic and sensitivity is unexplored

Utterance length confound: Paper acknowledges training increases utterance length; no analysis of whether improvements stem from persuasion or simply from verbosity providing more information; no length penalty during training

Limited and potentially ambiguous human evaluation: Only 16 participants with 5 games each; fewer votes received could indicate avoidance due to suspicion rather than successful persuasion; no qualitative assessment of how persuasive vs. manipulative agents appeared
Weak ablations: No ablation on using hidden role information during training; no ablation on Measurer quality; no cross-game transfer experiments; no comparison of GRPO to PPO/DPO

Foundational assumptions not validated: No evidence that local optimization of immediate next-player response optimizes global game outcomes; trade-offs between convincing next player and maintaining credibility with others unexplored

strengths: Clear and well-motivated presentation with effective illustrations of the core idea
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple games with thorough ablation studies and cross-LLM generalization testing
Practical two-stage architecture (API-based backend + fine-tuned open-source refiner) well-justified by empirical comparisons
Consistent positive results across diverse social deduction games and baselines
Detailed appendices with prompts, case studies, and implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Stackelberg game-theoretic framework is superficial: the implementation amounts to reward-based RL with a simple log probability difference, not genuine Stackelberg equilibrium computation or strategic analysis
Significant train-test mismatch: intent identification (Eq. 1) guides training but is absent during inference; gap addressed only post-hoc via cosine similarity (~27% misalignment in Table 6)

Reward function (Eq. 5) lacks theoretical motivation connecting persuasion-based probability optimization to actual win rate improvements; ablation shows Neg-Only provides no benefit, suggesting supervised learning on positives dominates

Measurer generalization concerns: Qwen2.5-72B is fixed follower during training but actual followers vary; Figure 5 shows substantial performance variation across LLMs (40-52% on Werewolf), contradicting 'model-agnostic' claims

No statistical significance testing reported; win rate improvements lack confidence intervals or binomial tests despite 500-match sample sizes; human evaluation with only 16 participants and no significance analysis
Acknowledged utterance length increase in limitations but not quantified, mitigated, or analyzed despite being a significant practical issue

Limited methodological novelty: applies existing GRPO algorithm with straightforward reward function; no comparisons to simpler baselines (direct fine-tuning on outcomes, supervised preference learning)

Training data comes from self-play with vanilla agents; distribution shift when playing against diverse opponents not analyzed; modest dataset size (~4000 instances per game) for language-based learning
Sotopia results are marginal (0.15 improvement on Goal score, <2% relative gain) without significance testing
Missing analysis of mechanisms: what linguistic patterns does the Refiner learn? When/why does the method fail? Case studies are cherry-picked successes, not systematic analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: persuasive communication in SDGs is an important and underexplored research gap
Sound application of Stackelberg competition framework to turn-based dialogue with clear theoretical justification
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 diverse environments (Werewolf, Avalon, ONUW, Sotopia) with consistent improvements
Thorough ablation studies including reward function variants, hyperparameter sensitivity (K), training data size, and cross-LLM generalization
Human evaluation demonstrating practical effectiveness (highest win rate, fewest human votes received)
Pragmatic two-stage architecture leveraging strengths of API-based and fine-tuned models
Quantitative analysis of persuasion effectiveness showing clear improvement trajectory during training (cosine similarity 0.53→0.73)
Clear presentation with effective figures and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing techniques (Stackelberg modeling, GRPO) to a new domain rather than introducing novel methods
Significant train-test information mismatch: uses unobservable role information r_{t+1} during training but not at test time, creating potential gap between training and evaluation

Measurer model dependency not validated: relies on Qwen2.5-72B to simulate follower responses, but no analysis of how Measurer accuracy affects training; potential reward signal corruption if simulation is inaccurate
Acknowledged verbosity problem unresolved: paper admits training produces longer utterances but only suggests future work, limiting practical applicability despite being a known weakness
Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; some improvements are modest and may not be statistically significant

Reward function design underexplored: simple summation over K responses lacks principled justification; K=3 somewhat arbitrary; no ablation on alternative reward formulations (weighted, contrastive, etc.)

Weaker generalization evidence: cross-LLM tests are inference-only with per-game retraining; true cross-domain transfer (train Werewolf→test Avalon) not explored; modest improvements on open-ended Sotopia tasks suggest limited generalizability
Measurer approximation during state changes: using G_t to approximate G_{t+1} during training could introduce significant bias when game states change
Case studies cherry-picked: only successful examples shown; no analysis of failure modes or conditions where persuasion backfires
Computational costs not analyzed: 50-hour training on 4×A800 GPUs and two-stage inference latency not discussed; practical deployment feasibility unclear
